Data quality — not uniform across the sample, and that's shown, not hidden

20 of the 26 firms run on dividend/split-adjusted returns with real daily high/low ranges, extended through 27 August 2026. Another 3 — OMV, Tenaris, Vår Energi — now run on properly dividend-adjusted returns too (via each firm's Total Return Index), though still without a real intraday range and with data only through 6 July 2026. Only TotalEnergies, Equinor, and Ørsted remain on the older, unadjusted close-to-close methodology, because updated source data for them hasn't been supplied yet. Every firm below is tagged with which basis its numbers rest on.

New: real green bond events, not simulated ones

The Green Bond Events tab holds 147 verified green bond issuances across 12 firms, pulled from two Bloomberg bond-screener exports (one dated 2019–2026 with issue dates and ISINs, cross-checked against an earlier active-bonds pull) and manually checked against false matches. Of those, 89 events across 11 issuers satisfy the dissertation's event-study data requirements (sufficient pre-event estimation history and event-window coverage) and form the validated sample: Enel's only verified bond predates the price series entirely, and one further Engie event (21/06/2019) cannot support the full 120-day pre-event window and is excluded on the same rule applied to every other candidate — not case-by-case. This is the first actual empirical test in this tracker, not a live-data illustration of the mechanic, and its headline result is consistent with the dissertation's own independent Python reconstruction of the same N=89 sample.

Mispricing Z-Score

20d CAR standardised against its own trailing 252-day distribution · |z| > 2 flagged as a significant deviation
Reading this chart: z-score measures how unusual the current abnormal-return drift is relative to the stock's own history, using the SXEP Index as the market-model benchmark — it flags where returns have diverged from what the model predicts, not a fundamental valuation. TotalEnergies, Equinor and Ørsted are computed from price returns only (no total-return/dividend series in this extract), so their AR is not directly comparable to the TRI-based firms. This is a return-based screening signal, not a substitute for the event-study CAAR test in the dissertation methodology.

Live Calculation — —

Market model, per-firm abnormal return, and rolling CAR — the exact three-step calculation behind every number on this page, worked through for the currently selected firm
Step 1 — Market Model (rolling 120-day estimation window)
Rᵢ,ₜ = αᵢ + βᵢ·Rₘ,ₜ + εᵢ,ₜ   (Rₘ = SXEP Index log return)
Step 2 — Abnormal Return
ARᵢ,ₜ = Rᵢ,ₜ − (α̂ᵢ + β̂ᵢ·Rₘ,ₜ)
Step 3 — Rolling 20-Day Cumulative Abnormal Return (this tracker's diagnostic)
CARᵢ(t−20,t) = Σ ARᵢ,ₜ   →   zᵢ,ₜ = (CARᵢ,ₜ − mean₂₅₂ₐ) / std₂₅₂ₐ
Dissertation's event-study CAAR (not computed here — needs dated events)
CAAR(τ₁,τ₂) = (1/N) Σᵢ CARᵢ(τ₁,τ₂)   — averaged across all N sample firms around an actual green-bond/transition-announcement date τ, tested against zero
Important distinction: the number this tracker shows live (CAR / z) is a rolling diagnostic — it recomputes every trading day using whatever the last 20 days looked like. Your dissertation's actual CAAR is event-anchored — computed only in a fixed window around each dated transition announcement, then averaged across firms and tested for statistical significance (t-test / Patell test) against the null of zero abnormal return. These are related but not the same statistic; this tracker cannot compute your real CAAR without the event calendar (announcement dates) loaded in, which isn't part of this Bloomberg price extract.

Definitions & Sources

Support / Resistance
A price level a stock has repeatedly failed to fall below (support) or rise above (resistance) recently. Computed here from the highest swing-high and lowest swing-low over the trailing ~6 months of weekly bars (Kirkpatrick & Dow, Technical Analysis: The Complete Resource).
Breakout
When price closes beyond a support or resistance line for the first time, signalling the range may be ending.
Fibonacci Retracement
Horizontal lines (23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8%, 78.6%) marking likely pause/reversal points within the current support–resistance range, based on ratios from the Fibonacci sequence. Widely used by technical traders; not derived from any fundamental relationship to the company.
Channel (Ascending / Descending)
Two roughly parallel diagonal lines — one fitted through recent swing highs, one through recent swing lows — bounding a stock that's trending steadily up or down. A close beyond either line is read the same way as a horizontal breakout: the first sign the trend inside the channel may be ending. This tracker fits both lines by linear regression through the same swing points used for horizontal support/resistance, then checks whether their slopes are close enough to count as "parallel."
Triangle (Ascending / Descending / Symmetrical)
Like a channel, but the two lines aren't parallel — they converge toward a point. A flat top over rising lows is an ascending triangle (bias to break upward); falling highs over a flat bottom is a descending triangle (bias to break downward); both lines sloping toward each other is a symmetrical triangle (no directional bias — the breakout direction is the signal, not the shape itself). Per Kirkpatrick & Dow's Technical Analysis: The Complete Resource, a triangle isn't "complete" until price actually closes beyond one of the two lines.
Hammer / Hanging Man
A candle with a small body at the top of its range and a lower shadow at least twice the body's height, with little or no upper shadow (Nison's "umbrella line"). The exact same shape means opposite things depending on what came before it: after a decline it's a hammer (bullish); after an advance it's a hanging man (bearish, and per Nison should wait for a lower close the next session before acting on it).
Shooting Star / Inverted Hammer
The mirror image of a hammer — a long upper shadow with the body near the low, minimal lower shadow. After an advance, it's a shooting star (bearish rejection of higher prices); after a decline, it's an inverted hammer (a tentative bullish signal that benefits from confirmation).
Engulfing Pattern
A two-candle reversal where the second body completely engulfs the first, opposite colour, after a clear prior trend. Nison's own technique: the high of a bearish engulfing pair becomes a resistance level, the low of a bullish engulfing pair becomes a support level — this tracker draws that level automatically for the most recent hit.
Dark Cloud Cover / Piercing Line
Two-candle reversals where the second candle opens beyond the first's extreme, then closes back through more than half of the first candle's body — dark cloud cover is the bearish version (after an uptrend), piercing line the bullish version (after a downtrend). The deeper the close pushes into the prior body, the stronger the signal.
Harami
A small body sitting entirely inside the prior session's much larger, opposite-coloured body. Read as the market stalling after a strong move — indecision, not a firm reversal signal on its own.
Doji
Open and close are essentially equal. On its own it's a caution flag that the prior trend may be losing momentum, not a directional signal.
Moving Average (MA) as Support/Resistance
A single moving-average line can act as a dynamic floor while a stock trends up (price keeps bouncing off it) or a dynamic ceiling while it trends down (price keeps getting rejected by it) — the "MA Role" readout above detects which is currently happening.
RSI (Relative Strength Index)
A 0–100 momentum gauge; readings above 70 are conventionally read as overbought, below 30 as oversold.
Bollinger Bands
A 20-day average price ± 2 standard deviations, showing whether a stock is trading in an unusually wide or narrow range relative to its own recent history.
Mispricing Z-Score
How unusual a stock's 20-day abnormal-return drift is relative to its own trailing 252-day history — see the Live Tracker tab for the full formula.
Which benchmark, and when
SXEP Index is the only benchmark used inside the actual mispricing calculation (the market-model regression). Brent crude and Dutch TTF gas are optional overlays, shown only for firms where they're actually relevant to the business.
A note on the candlesticks
These weekly bars are built from daily closing prices (open = week's first close, high/low = week's max/min close, close = week's last close) — not true intraday OHLC data. Pattern-reading here is illustrative, not tradable-grade.

The dissertation's own formulas, computed live on real data

Every calculation below is genuinely re-computed in your browser from the actual price data in this tracker — nothing here is a static example. Pick a firm, and each step recalculates using that firm's real numbers, in the exact order the dissertation's methodology chapter uses them: raw return → market model → abnormal return → cumulative abnormal return (CAR) → averaged across all firms (CAAR) → tested for significance → applied to a real announcement window (H1/H2). Each step's output is literally what the next step's formula uses as its input — that's the algorithm.

Reading Key — what a value actually tells you

ValueRoughly normalWorth noticingWhat it's telling you
β (beta)0.5 – 1.5>1.5 or <0.3How much the stock swings relative to the sector. β=1 moves with SXEP; β=2 moves twice as hard in both directions.
AR (one day)within ±1%beyond ±3%A single day's "unexplained" move. Small numbers are just noise — expected almost every day.
CAR (20 days)within ±3%beyond ±8%Noise adds up over a month; a large, one-directional CAR means something has been consistently pushing the price, not random wobble.
t-statistic−2 to +2beyond ±2Below 2 in magnitude: could easily be chance. Above 2: this pattern would occur by chance less than ~5% of the time.
ρ̂ (autocorrelation)near 0, below thresholdabove the threshold shownWhether one day's abnormal return predicts the next day's. Near zero is what efficient pricing predicts.

Real green bond events, EU energy & utilities sector

Everything on this tab is compiled from a Bloomberg bond-screener export (global active green bonds, cross-checked issuer by issuer to remove false matches — an early pass wrongly caught Nordea Bank Abp, Banco BPM and others under a loose "BP" search; those are excluded here). This isn't a demonstration of the methodology — it's the first genuine empirical test this tracker has run.

Context for why this matters specifically for this sample: European energy and utility issuers sit at the center of the EU's transition-finance push — the EU Taxonomy, SFDR, and the broader post-Paris shift in how capital is allocated toward decarbonisation all point capital-raising activity at exactly this sector. Whether that activity gets priced efficiently or with a lag is the empirical question this dissertation asks, and the results below are a first, small-sample look at an actual answer.

RPreliminary Event Study — CAAR and Significance Tests

N=89 across 11 issuers (Ørsted, Nordex, Siemens Energy, RWE, Iberdrola, EDP, SSE, Neste, Engie, Snam, PKN Orlen) — the validated event-study sample, not the broader 147-event verified calendar. Enel is excluded entirely: its only verified green bond (16/01/2018) predates the 2019-01-02 start of the price series, so no 120-day estimation window can be constructed for it. One further candidate event — Engie, 21/06/2019 — is excluded on the identical rule: its required pre-event history would begin before the common return data starts, and extending one firm's history selectively to keep it would apply a different inclusion rule to a single event. N falls further to 88 in the two widest windows ([−5,+10], [−10,+10]) only, where one issuer lacks sufficient trading history for that offset — a window-length constraint, not a further bond-matching or data gap.

Estimated using a 120-day market-model window ending 12 trading days before each event date, with abnormal returns summed into CAR for each window and averaged into CAAR across events. Two significance tests are reported: a cross-sectional t-test (mean / [SD/√N]) and a Patell (1976) standardized-residual Z-test, which weights each event's CAR by the inverse of its own estimation-period residual volatility before aggregating.

WindowNCAARt-statPatell ZPositiveRead
Result (N=89, 11 issuers): CAAR is negative across all six windows, from −0.19% at [0,+1] to roughly −1.1% to −1.2% at [−5,+10] (N=88 at this window; see note above). The primary [−1,+1] window gives CAAR ≈ −0.41%, t ≈ −1.33, Patell Z ≈ −0.96 — none of which clears conventional significance, consistent with the dissertation's own independently reconstructed figure of −0.4131% (t=−1.34, Patell Z=−1.15, p=.250). The widest window, [−5,+10], is the one place a test crosses the raw 5% threshold (Patell Z ≈ −2.0–2.2); the dissertation reports this does not survive Holm-Bonferroni correction for testing six windows at once (adjusted p ≈ .134), so it should not be read as a significant result once that correction is applied. H1 is therefore rejected on direction — the sign is consistently negative, not the positive signalling effect the hypothesis predicts — but not established on magnitude: none of the six windows is statistically distinguishable from zero once multiple testing is accounted for. The result runs counter to the significant positive reaction reported in Flammer (2021); the dissertation reads this as evidence that a green label alone does not generate a uniform positive equity response in a later, more transition-intensive sample, not as proof of a negative valuation effect. Scope note: the cross-sectional determinants of this pattern (issuer transition-exposure tier, financing size, first-issuance status) are tested separately below (H3a/H3b) — bond-level characteristics explain almost nothing, while issuer identity produces the sharpest contrast in the whole analysis.

Independent validation: the dissertation separately reconstructs this event study in Python, using a separately obtained Bloomberg data pull and independently written code (Appendix B). That reconstruction also converges on N=89 across the same 11 issuers, with CAAR(-1,+1) = −0.413% (t ≈ −1.34) — the live computation on this tab is built from this tracker's own data pipeline, not copied from that reconstruction, and its landing in the same place (≈−0.41%, N=89, same non-significant conclusion) is itself a form of cross-implementation agreement rather than a coincidence.

RBenchmark Robustness — SXEP vs. SXKP for the 4 "High Transition" Firms

Ørsted, Nordex, Siemens Energy and RWE are the tracker's clearest transition pure-plays/pivots — arguably a worse fit for SXEP (oil & gas) than any other subsample. This checks their results against SXKP (STOXX Europe 600 Renewable Energy), a properly sector-matched benchmark. 19 events, same methodology, only the market index changes.
WindowNCAAR (SXEP)t-stat (SXEP)CAAR (SXKP)t-stat (SXKP)
CAAR(-1,+1)19-1.46%-1.89-1.40%-1.56
CAAR(0,+5)19-0.88%-0.85-0.81%-0.71
CAAR(-5,+10)19-1.99%-1.05-1.23%-0.60

Direction and magnitude are robust to benchmark choice; significance is not. Under SXKP, all three windows retain the sign and approximate magnitude of the SXEP result — the tightest window changes by only 0.06 percentage points (−1.46% vs −1.40%). The t-statistic weakens under the sector-matched benchmark (−1.89 → −1.56 at [−1,+1]), consistent with SXKP absorbing some of the common variation SXEP leaves as apparent signal. A result that survives a benchmark switch economically but falls short of significance under both is the strongest evidence in this analysis of a real, if modest, effect specific to high-transition-exposure issuers.

Issuance size and beta both correlate weakly with every CAR window (|r| ≤ 0.15), indicating no systematic relationship between deal size or firm risk sensitivity and market reaction magnitude in this sample. The three CAR windows correlate moderately with each other (0.53–0.62), which is a mechanical consequence of overlapping day ranges (e.g. [0,+5] and [−5,+10] share several days with [−1,+1]) rather than an independent finding — the six windows should be read as overlapping views of one abnormal-return series, not six independent tests.

RBenchmark Robustness — SXEP vs. SX6P for the 6 Pure Utility Firms

EDP, Enel, Engie, Iberdrola, RWE, SSE are utilities, not oil & gas producers — this checks whether their results depend on using SXEP (STOXX Europe 600 Oil & Gas), the benchmark used everywhere else in this tracker, versus SX6P (STOXX Europe 600 Utilities), the sector-matched alternative. 68 events, same market-model methodology, same estimation window, only the benchmark index changes.
WindowNCAAR (SXEP)t-stat (SXEP)CAAR (SX6P)t-stat (SX6P)
CAAR(-1,+1)68-0.24%-0.71-0.22%*-0.82*
CAAR(0,+5)68-0.50%-0.98-0.41%*-1.31*
CAAR(-5,+10)67-1.03%-1.37-0.08%*-0.16*

The two tight windows ([−1,+1] and [0,+5]) are robust to benchmark choice: both indices agree on sign and magnitude, and both remain non-significant. The wide window ([−5,+10]) is not robust — SXEP shows a −0.93% drift that SX6P reduces to −0.08%, a difference attributable to divergent sector-level movements between oil & gas and utility indices over a 16-day window. The immediate-to-medium-term result should be reported as robust; the 16-day result should be reported with this caveat rather than as an unqualified finding.

RPlacebo Test — Matched Pseudo-Event Dates

For each of the 89 events, a pool of placebo dates was built from the same firm's trading days within the same calendar year, excluding any date within 10 calendar days of a genuine issuance, and requiring the same 120-day estimation window and [-1,+1] event window used throughout. 1,000 Monte Carlo draws each sampled one placebo CAR per firm and averaged across all 89 firms, building an empirical null distribution of "CAAR on an arbitrary, non-issuance day."
StatisticValue
Actual CAAR(-1,+1)-0.41%
Mean placebo CAAR+0.01%
Placebo standard deviation0.30%
95% placebo interval[-0.58%, +0.62%]
Two-sided empirical p-value0.163

The actual CAAR falls inside the 95% placebo interval, and the two-sided empirical p-value (0.163) does not indicate the actual result is extreme relative to an arbitrary non-event day for these firms. This is consistent with, not contradicting, the non-significant parametric and non-parametric results throughout — on every test applied, the negative CAAR is directionally consistent but not statistically distinguishable from the kind of variation these firms' returns show on an ordinary trading day. The placebo pool is restricted to the same firm and calendar year as each real event (controlling for firm- and year-specific volatility regimes) rather than a fully unrestricted random-date design across the whole sample and period — a natural extension for further precision.

RH3a — Heterogeneity by Transition-Exposure Tier

A dissertation-constructed, theoretically motivated classification of each issuer's business-model centrality to the energy transition — not an externally reported accounting variable or ESG score. Categorical by design: the distance between Tier 1 and Tier 2 isn't assumed equal to the distance between Tier 2 and Tier 3.
TierInterpretationIssuersNMean CAR(-1,+1)
Tier 1Transition/renewable activity central to productive assets and business transformationØrsted, Nordex, Siemens Energy, RWE19-1.46%
Tier 2Diversified operating model, substantial renewable activity, financially materialIberdrola, EDP, SSE, Neste44-0.04%
Tier 3Meaningful transition activity alongside substantial conventional energy/gas/refiningEngie, Snam, PKN Orlen26-0.28%
This is the sharpest cross-sectional result in the whole analysis — pooling issuers, as the aggregate CAAR above does, hides it entirely. Tier 1's −1.46% is economically the largest and most negative estimate anywhere in this tab, and it holds up under a sector-matched renewable-energy benchmark (SXKP instead of SXEP), moving only from −1.46% to −1.40%. The formal Welch t-test comparing Tier 1 against Tier 2 is −1.69 (p=.102) — not significant at conventional levels, which is a direct consequence of N=19 rather than evidence the pattern isn't real: a visually large, internally consistent effect on the smallest subsample is exactly the profile a larger follow-up sample would be best placed to confirm or overturn. Read together with H3b below, the pattern is that issuer identity (how central transition is to the business) predicts the market reaction far better than any single bond's own characteristics — the market appears to price who is issuing, not what is being issued.

RH3b — Financing Characteristics, Firm-Clustered Regression

CAR(-1,+1) regressed on FirstIssuance (earliest verified issuance by that issuer in-sample) and ln(Amount, EUR), with issuance amounts matched directly against the raw Bloomberg bond-export files and converted to EUR using the historical spot exchange rate on each event's actual issue date — not an annual average. Runs on the complete validated sample, N=89, 11 firm clusters — every one of the 89 events carries both a matched Bloomberg bond record and a complete EUR-standardised amount, so no further exclusions apply here.
VariableCoefficientClustered SEClustered p
FirstIssuance-0.9131.177.438
ln(Amount, EUR)-0.4850.364.183

Neither coefficient reaches conventional significance (N=89, 11 firm clusters). Both signs run against the naive signalling prediction that bigger or first-time issues should provoke a stronger reaction — if anything the point estimates go the other way, though neither is distinguishable from zero. The unconditional correlations tell the same story before any regression is run: CAR correlates -0.10 with logged issue size and comparably weakly with FirstIssuance (see the pairwise correlation table above), both close enough to zero to rule out a masked bivariate relationship the multivariate model is somehow obscuring. H3b is therefore not supported, and — read against H3a above — that null is the useful complement rather than a separate disappointment: bond-level attributes (size, novelty) explain almost nothing, while issuer-level identity (transition tier) produces the sharpest contrast in the whole analysis. With only 11 firm clusters, cluster-robust standard errors rely on asymptotics known to be unreliable at this cluster count; a wild cluster bootstrap would be the appropriate confirmatory step, though with both coefficients already non-significant, it would mainly be informative if it materially narrowed either estimate.

What to actually watch for — and where — for your event calendar

This section isn't decoration; it maps directly onto Section 3.1.2's event-identification rules. Two different jobs, two different kinds of source:

Watch forWhy it mattersWhere to check
Green bond / SLB issuanceYour core event type — the actual announcements CAR/CAAR is measured around.Climate Bonds Initiative database — your dissertation's own primary event-date source (Section 3.1.2)
Transition-strategy / capex announcementsBroader than a bond issuance — a capital-allocation shift toward renewables/decarbonisation is still a transition signal even with no debt instrument attached.Each firm's own Investor Relations press-release page — the most authoritative, least delayed source; always cross-check the exact first-public-disclosure date against news coverage
Earnings announcement datesYour confounding-event exclusion rule (Section 3.1.2.i) — an event window can't be trusted if an earnings release lands inside it, since you can't separate the two effects.Company IR calendar page, or a WRDS/Bloomberg earnings-calendar pull — needed before you finalise which transition announcements are usable events
Sector-wide macro newsDistinguishes a firm-specific mispricing signal from a commodity-risk repricing — exactly the Brent/TTF overlay logic on the Live Tracker tab.Reuters Energy, Bloomberg Energy — check the date of any large oil/gas price move against your event dates before attributing a CAR to the transition announcement itself
Regulatory deadlines (EU Taxonomy, SFDR, CSRD)These often *cause* clusters of announcements — several firms disclosing around the same compliance deadline, which is exactly the calendar-clustering issue Brown & Warner (1985) flag for cross-sectional dependence (see the Methodology tab, Step 11).European Commission sustainable-finance pages; useful for explaining why events cluster, not for individual event dates

Practical order of operations: pull the CBI database first for your core green-bond/SLB event list → cross-check each date against the issuer's own IR release (CBI's recorded date is sometimes the pricing date, not the first public announcement — they can differ by days) → pull each firm's earnings calendar and drop any event where the two dates fall within your event window → only then run the CAR/CAAR machinery from the Methodology tab on what's left.

Why this isn't a live embedded Yahoo Finance feed

A static HTML file like this one can't pull live data from finance.yahoo.com directly: Yahoo blocks cross-origin requests from arbitrary pages (no public free API for client-side use) and blocks being embedded in an iframe at all (X-Frame-Options). There's no backend server here to proxy around that. What does work, and is below: (1) direct links straight to each firm's live Yahoo Finance page, which opens real, current data in a new tab; (2) a curated snapshot of real, current headlines relevant to the sample, gathered and paraphrased as of early August 2026 — these won't update on their own, but every link is real and goes to the original source.

Why 2019, and why these 26 names

Why the window starts in January 2019: the dissertation's own data section states coverage "from January 2019 to the present," giving roughly 1,955–1,956 trading days per firm. Practically, that's driven by the estimation-window requirement in the market model itself — the dissertation specifies a 120-trading-day estimation window ending 11 days before each event date ([−130,−11], following MacKinlay 1997 and Riaz et al. 2025), so the sample needs several years of pre-event history to have enough usable events at all. Substantively, 2019 also sits just before the EU Green Deal (announced December 2019) and the first real wave of energy-sector green bond and sustainability-linked financing — so the window captures a "before" baseline alongside the acceleration of transition-finance activity, plus two major exogenous shocks (the 2020 Covid oil-price collapse and the 2021–22 European gas crisis) that the dissertation's confounding-event exclusion rules and this tracker's macro overlays both have to account for.

Sample rationale. The research question concerns whether transition-finance announcements generate abnormal returns consistent with delayed information incorporation rather than instantaneous, efficient repricing (Section 1.3). Testing this requires cross-sectional variation in transition exposure: firms with minimal exposure (Tenaris, Vallourec — oilfield equipment, limited renewables activity) through to firms whose core business is the transition itself (Vestas, Nordex, Siemens Energy, and functionally Ørsted). The supermajors (BP, Shell, Eni, TotalEnergies, Equinor) represent the highest-profile transition announcers; the mid-cap services and infrastructure names (Saipem, Subsea 7, Enagás, Snam, GTT, Vopak) test whether the same pricing pattern holds for less-scrutinised, lower-liquidity issuers, where information frictions are expected to be more pronounced (NGFS, 2022).

Six utilities added subsequently (EDP, Enel, Engie, Iberdrola, RWE, SSE) extend price coverage for firms with already-verified green bond issuances, closing a data gap rather than expanding sample scope. They occupy a defensible position on the same transition-exposure spectrum: RWE has committed to a renewables target of 65GW by 2030 (up from ~16GW in 2023), backed by a €55bn capital programme and a scheduled coal exit — a repositioning comparable in scale to Ørsted's. Iberdrola, EDP and Enel are each built around renewables-heavy generation portfolios (Iberdrola Renovables, EDP Renováveis, Enel Green Power). Engie and SSE occupy a more central position — Engie retains substantial gas-infrastructure exposure alongside renewables investment, and SSE has divested UK retail supply to concentrate on transmission and renewables. Firm-level renewable-capacity and capex figures should be sourced from each company's own annual report or sustainability disclosures rather than cited from this summary.

Why the benchmarks (SXEP, CO1, TZT1): SXEP (STOXX Europe 600 Oil & Gas) is not optional — it is the literal R(m,t) term in the dissertation's own abnormal-return formula, AR(i,t) = R(i,t) − [α̂ + β̂·R(m,t)], so every CAR and z-score in this tracker is computed against it directly. Brent crude (CO1) and Dutch TTF gas (TZT1) sit outside that regression — they're included as interpretive overlays, because the dissertation's central tension (Section 1.1) is distinguishing risk-based repricing (Bolton & Kacperczyk, 2021: carbon/commodity risk earns a return premium) from mispricing-based delayed incorporation (Atilgan et al., 2023). If a firm's abnormal-return spike lines up with a Brent or TTF move, that's a flag the effect may be commodity-risk-driven rather than transition-signal-driven — exactly the ambiguity the dissertation is built to resolve, and exactly what the overlay toggles on the Live Tracker tab are for.

Will this actually help you understand mispricing patterns? Yes, in the sense that it turns your raw Bloomberg extract into something you can look at and reason about — spotting which names currently show the largest abnormal-return drift, whether that drift coincides with a macro move, and whether trend/momentum readings corroborate or contradict the mispricing signal. It is a research and sanity-checking tool, not a validated result — see the Technical Analysis tab for the fuller list of what would need to change before anything here could inform an actual trade.

What this tracker is actually for — and why "short-term" is the point

Most transition-finance and ESG research asks a long-term question: do sustainable firms outperform over years or decades? Your dissertation asks a different, narrower question — when a specific transition-related announcement hits the market, does the price adjust immediately (efficient) or does it drift over the following days and weeks (mispricing)? That's inherently a short-horizon question, because the whole test depends on watching what happens in a tight window (your event study uses [-2,+5], [-2,+10] day windows) around a dated event — not what a stock does over five years.

That's the actual purpose of this tracker: it's a way to see that short-horizon dynamic — the 20-day rolling CAR and the z-score — across all 26 names at once, continuously, rather than only at the handful of event dates in your formal study. It facilitates the process by turning "is there unusual short-term return behaviour right now, and does it look macro-driven or firm-specific" into something visual and immediate, instead of something you'd only find by rerunning the regression by hand for each firm.

On "alpha generation" and actually making money from mispricing: academically, if your dissertation finds that transition announcements produce a statistically significant post-announcement drift (underreaction) rather than an instant jump, the textbook implication is a momentum-style strategy — go long firms showing significant positive CAR drift after a transition event, short (or avoid) those showing negative drift, holding only over the drift window before it's expected to close. That is the theoretical channel by which "mispricing" becomes "alpha": you are being paid for correctly identifying delayed information incorporation, not for taking on extra risk (per the Atilgan et al. framing your dissertation already uses).

In practice, turning that into real money is a much bigger step than this tool provides: it requires (i) confirming the drift is statistically significant and not just noise in a 26-name sample, (ii) checking it survives realistic transaction costs and bid-ask spreads — small/mid-cap European names like Vallourec or SBM Offshore are far more expensive to trade than BP or Shell, (iii) out-of-sample and walk-forward testing, since an in-sample pattern is not a forward guarantee, and (iv) position sizing and risk management this tracker does not attempt. This is exactly the gap the Technical Analysis tab's answer card already flags — worth treating this as the diagnostic layer that would sit underneath a real strategy, not as the strategy itself.

On "which one is currently worth it": the Total Return and Sharpe columns now in the Live Tracker table give you an honest, computed answer to "which names had the best risk-adjusted historical return over 2019–2026" — that's a fact about the past, not a prediction. I'm not going to tell you which stock to buy today; what the data can tell you is which names combined high return with low volatility historically, and you can weigh that against the current mispricing z-score and technical trend yourself.

The sample comprises 23 core European energy & utility firms extracted from Bloomberg, chosen to maximise cross-sectional variation in exposure to the oil-to-green transition — from names with essentially no transition exposure (Tenaris, Vallourec) to names whose entire business model is the transition (Vestas, Nordex, Siemens Energy). Three supplementary single-name references (TotalEnergies, Equinor, Ørsted) were added as price-only series, alongside two macro commodity benchmarks (Brent crude, Dutch TTF gas) and the SXEP Index used as the market-model benchmark. Six further utilities (EDP, Enel, Engie, Iberdrola, RWE, SSE) were added later with their own price history specifically to compute real CAR for their already-verified green bond issuances — see the rationale below.
